newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper announces new push for peace.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper announces new push for peace.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper said on Monday he was pressing ahead with plans to launch new talks to end Colombia's 30-year-old guerrilla uprising and hoped to make contact with rebel leaders within the next 60 days.

The announcement, in a televised address, came as the army prepared to send 5,000 troops back into the southern jungles after temporarily ceding a huge zone to Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels, permitting them to free 70 troops, some of whom they held prisoner for almost 10 months.

"I have asked Daniel Garcia Pena (high commissioner for peace) and presidential adviser Jose Noe Rios ... to establish within the next 60 days the necessary contacts with armed groups to define the terms and conditions under which we could hold the first peace talks," Samper said.
"My vocation (as president) has and will continue being to sow the seed of peace ... though it is possible that this desire will not be achieved during my mandate," he added.

Calls for a new peace process came after the FARC handed over the 70 captive troops in a public ceremony in the central square of Cartagena del Chaira, the main town in the demilitarized zone, on June 15.
Those calls were backed by some of the country's most influential industrialists in an open letter to Samper at the end of last week.

But the path to peace is likely to be rocky. Armed forces chief Gen. Harold Bedoya branded the troop handover a "circus with many clowns," while army commander Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett said the "agents of violence" must be defeated before peace could take root.

At the release ceremony, Cmdr. Joaquin Gomez, head of the FARC's so-called Southern Bloc, read a communique from the rebel army's supreme leader Manuel "Sureshot" Marulanda in which he set out a series of conditions for eventual negotiations with the Samper administration.
These included the demilitarization of other areas of the country and demands that right-wing paramilitary groups should first be disbanded.

In Monday night's speech, Samper said it still had to be decided whether to allow paramilitary groups to join the talks, adding: "(These initial contacts) are an exploratory mission, the results of which will determine whether or not we continue."
Last week, however, he ruled out demilitarizing other areas.

As the army geared up to return to the 5,000 square mile (13,000 sq km) demilitarized zone of Caqueta after a 32-day absence, Gen. Agustin Ardila, head of the army's Fourth Division, said: "I will restart operations (from midnight Monday) to consolidate (control) of the area which we won back from the narco-subversives at great cost ... This is not going to be a D-Day-style landing ... I'm under no pressure of time," he added.
Ardila said he would deploy an elite unit of special forces in the area, together with crack counterinsurgency troops backed by a small fleet of helicopter gunships and Navy river boats.
